title: Async & Promises
description: From callbacks to async generators — understand how TypeScript types asynchronous code at every level.

challenges.title: What does async return?
challenges.whyMatters: Every external call — HTTP requests, database queries, file reads — is async. Knowing what an async function returns prevents you from accidentally using a Promise where you need a value.
hints: async functions always return a Promise, even if you return a plain value

challenges.title: await unwraps the Promise
challenges.whyMatters: await strips the Promise wrapper — this is the basic mental model you need for every async operation in production tooling.
hints: await removes one layer of Promise<T> to give you T

challenges.title: Write your first async function
challenges.description:
Write an async function `delay(ms: number): Promise<void>` that resolves after `ms` milliseconds.

Then write `delayedGreeting(name: string, ms: number): Promise<string>` that waits `ms` milliseconds and then returns `"Hello, {name}!"`.
challenges.whyMatters: Delay utilities are used in retry loops, rate limiters, and health check polling — common patterns in any software engineering automation script.
hints: In delayedGreeting, await delay(ms) before returning the string

challenges.title: Typed error handling
challenges.whyMatters: Errors in async code are caught as unknown in strict TypeScript — you must narrow before using them. This trips up everyone the first time.
hints: TypeScript can't know what was thrown — it could be anything

challenges.title: Promise.all — parallel execution
challenges.description:
What does `Promise.all` do differently from awaiting each promise sequentially?

  // Sequential (await each)
  const a = await fetchA()  // waits 1s
  const b = await fetchB()  // then waits 1s → total: 2s

  // Parallel
  const [a, b] = await Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB()])  // total: 1s

And if fetchB() rejects, what happens?
challenges.whyMatters: Checking multiple services, fetching multiple config sources, or running parallel health checks — Promise.all is your tool. Knowing its failure behavior prevents silent partial results.
hints: Promise.all rejects as soon as any promise rejects

choices.label: fetchA result is returned, fetchB error is ignored
Promise.all rejects immediately with fetchB's error
Both errors are collected into an array
Promise.all waits for all to settle regardless

challenges.title: Write a parallel health checker
challenges.description:
Write a function `checkAll(urls: string[]): Promise<{ url: string; ok: boolean }[]>`

It should check all URLs in parallel (not sequentially). For this exercise, simulate each check with a function `ping(url: string): Promise<boolean>` that is already imported.

Return results for ALL urls — even if some fail. Use `Promise.allSettled` so one failure doesn't abort the rest.
challenges.whyMatters: This is a real health check pattern. You want results for all services, not an abort on the first failure. Promise.allSettled is the correct tool here over Promise.all.
hints: Map over urls, call ping(url) for each, pass all to Promise.allSettled
Narrow each result: result.status === 'fulfilled' to access result.value

challenges.title: AbortController — cancellation
challenges.whyMatters: Timeout-aware HTTP calls are mandatory in production production tooling — a hanging fetch will block your entire health check loop.
hints: AbortController has a .signal property that is passed to the options object

challenges.title: Write a timeout-aware fetch wrapper
challenges.description:
Write a function `fetchWithTimeout(url: string, timeoutMs: number): Promise<string>`

It should:
1. Create an AbortController
2. Set a timeout that aborts after `timeoutMs`
3. Fetch the URL with the signal
4. Return the response body as text
5. If aborted, throw an Error with message `"Request timed out: {url}"`
6. Clear the timeout if the fetch succeeds (to avoid memory leaks)

For testing purposes, `fetch` is provided as a global mock.
challenges.whyMatters: Every external HTTP call in your production tooling needs a timeout. This wrapper is something you'd write on day one of a new service.
hints: Wrap in try/finally — clearTimeout(timer) goes in finally
Check if error is an AbortError: err instanceof Error && err.name === 'AbortError'

challenges.title: Async generators — concept
challenges.whyMatters: Log streaming, Kubernetes event watching, and large file processing all use async generators — you read one item at a time instead of loading everything into memory.
hints: async function* with yield produces values one at a time on demand

choices.label: Prints all three lines at once after the loop
Prints 'a', then 'b', then 'c' — one per iteration
Throws because you can't use for..of with async
